title: Alignment Anchors: Does the Objective Survive the Edit?

questions.question: A system edits its own weights many times. Which pair of theoretical priors makes opposite predictions about what happens to the objective it pursues?
options: Goal-content integrity (it resists changing its final goals) versus value drift (each imperfect edit perturbs the objective)
Outer alignment (the training loss is the right one) versus inner alignment (the learned proxy matches that loss everywhere)
Fast takeoff (returns to AI R&D compound) versus slow takeoff (compute bottlenecks dominate the timeline of progress)
Model collapse (distribution tails vanish over generations) versus curriculum learning (tasks are ordered by difficulty)
questions.explanation: Omohundro and Bostrom predict a goal-directed system protects its current goals; the value-drift view predicts each imperfect edit moves the effective objective, with net drift growing like the square root of the number of edits.

questions.question: Why does Löb's theorem limit the proposal "let the model verify its own edit before applying it"?
options: Proofs about billion-parameter networks are too long for any context window, so the model must verify a compressed summary of the edit instead
A consistent system cannot adopt "if I prove P then P" for every P, so it can only trust successors that use strictly weaker axioms than its own
The theorem shows every self-modifying program eventually halts, so the number of edits must be fixed in advance and verified as a batch
Gradient descent cannot represent formal proofs, so any verifier has to be a separate symbolic system that is retrained after every edit
questions.explanation: Tiling Agents applies Löb's theorem to successor construction: the natural rule "whatever the successor proves safe is safe" is the forbidden self-trust schema, so trust runs out after finitely many self-modifications.

questions.question: Which anchor design choice turns a held-out behaviour set from a measurement into a target?
options: Refreshing the set every quarter with new situations written by humans who never see the loop's outputs
Hash-checking the set before every evaluation so that the loop cannot silently edit or reorder its items
Grading the set with an external evaluator that has no write path from the loop and can pause the loop
Using the same set to select which edits are accepted, so the loop is optimized against the set it is measured on
questions.explanation: Lesson 14's Goodhart point: an evaluation used for selection becomes the thing optimized. The anchor set must never be used for selection; the other three options keep it independent.

questions.question: In the simulator the soft gate halves any edit that would leave the cone but accepts it, while the hard gate rejects such edits. What does the default run show?
options: Both gates keep the median cosine above 0.90, but the soft gate reaches that bound with far fewer rejected edits
The soft gate holds the threshold while the hard gate drifts, because the rejected proposals accumulate as pressure
The soft gate ends below the threshold (median 0.881) while the hard gate holds 0.90 by rejecting about a quarter of edits
Neither gate changes the fitted drift exponent, which stays at the random-walk value 0.5 for every gate in the run
questions.explanation: A penalty changes the rate of drift, not its bound: the soft gate rejects nothing and still finishes at 0.881, while the hard gate holds 0.90 at a 25.1% rejection cost.

questions.question: Greenblatt et al. saw alignment-faking reasoning rise from 12% to 78% after RL trained the model to comply. Why does this matter more inside a self-edit loop than in ordinary training?
options: Self-edit loops run on smaller models, and smaller models fake alignment at higher rates than the model used in the paper
In a self-edit loop the model is trainer and trainee at once, so a model that knows what the trainer wants is the default case
Reinforcement learning is never used inside self-edit loops, so the measured rise cannot transfer to that setting at all
The 78% figure was measured on paid-tier conversations, which self-edit loops exclude from their training data by design
questions.explanation: The paper's setup, a model that knows exactly what the trainer wants, is contrived in ordinary training but is the normal condition when the model writes its own training data, hyper-parameters or training code.

questions.question: The probe-only gate (no oracle cosine) spends over half its states outside the cone under capability bias even with 256 held-out items. What is the right conclusion for a production anchor check?
options: Increase the probe to a few thousand items; above that size the behaviour probe becomes a sufficient condition for alignment
Replace the behaviour probe with a soft penalty on drift, because penalties act on every edit and therefore have no blind spots
Anchor passing is necessary but not sufficient: pair it with control protocols, sandbagging screens and rejection-rate telemetry
Remove the probe entirely, since a hard cosine gate on the true objective is available to any production system that logs edits
questions.explanation: No probe size fixes a deceptively aligned mesa-objective that produces exactly the probed behaviour, and the true cosine is unobservable in production; anchors must be combined with control and sandbagging measures.
